finding.claim: The iconUrl value from the PUT /profile request is stored without any validation. The nightly sync job later fetches it server-side with a GET. An attacker can point it at internal services, such as cloud metadata at http://169.254.169.254/ or localhost admin endpoints, or at arbitrary hosts. The response body is read as a byte array, so it may be exposed if the icon is served back.
finding.source: icon parameter of Profile.update (PUT /profile handler), line 11
finding.sink: HttpClient.send with HttpRequest GET to URI.create(iconUrl), lines 23-24

trace.note: update(webhook, icon): icon is attacker-controlled request input
this.iconUrl = icon, stored with no scheme, host or IP validation
sync() builds a GET request to URI.create(iconUrl) and sends it with HttpClient

finding.guards_checked: No validation is applied to iconUrl. There is no scheme or host allowlist and no private-IP or metadata-address blocking. The regex check at line 12 covers only the webhook parameter. The HttpClient is passed in, so its redirect and proxy configuration is unknown.

verdict.guard_found: none (the regex at src/Profile.java:12 validates only the webhook parameter, not icon)
verdict.reason: src/Profile.java:11 takes icon from the PUT handler, :16 stores it with no validation, and :23 fetches URI.create(iconUrl) via HttpClient GET. The only check, at :12, covers webhook alone, so a closing guard does not exist. No other callers or validation exist in the codebase. The finding's claim that the response may be exposed is unverified, because nothing here serves the bytes back, but the blind SSRF request itself is confirmed.
